title: Wind Energy Fundamentals
desc: Learn how wind turbines turn wind into power, how sites are assessed, and the safety, cost and community basics.
outcomes: Explain how a turbine converts wind into electricity.
Estimate energy from wind speed and rotor size.
Judge cost, noise, wildlife and safety.
Write a simple feasibility note for a small wind project.
task: Produce a feasibility note for a small wind installation, with a wind data table, energy estimate, cost and payback, safety and community checks.
condition: A computer, public wind data for a chosen site, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor engineer. No work at height is done in this course.
standard: Energy estimate uses stated formulas and units; payback is calculated in your currency; safety and community points are listed; assumptions are written; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Technicians, engineering students, community energy groups, small farm owners.
evidence: wind data table, energy and payback sheet, safety checklist, feasibility note
modules: How a wind turbine works
Understand
A wind turbine turns the push of moving air into electricity. Knowing the parts and the physics helps you judge any project.
Blades capture wind and turn a shaft; a generator converts rotation to electricity; a tower lifts the rotor into stronger wind; a controller manages speed and safety.
Key speeds: cut-in (starts), rated (full power) and cut-out (stops for safety).
Power grows with the cube of wind speed, so a small increase in speed gives a large increase in power.
Larger blades sweep more area, which also raises power.
Doubling the wind speed from 5 to 10 m/s gives about eight times more power. A turbine producing 1 kW at 5 m/s could produce about 8 kW at 10 m/s, until it reaches its rated power.
Label a turbine diagram and write one sentence on what each part does.
All main parts are named and the cube rule is stated correctly.
Wind resource and sites
Analyse
Good wind makes or breaks a project, and wind data decides whether to continue.
Wind speed rises with height; trees, buildings and hills cause turbulence.
Use at least a year of hourly or ten-minute averages from a mast or a trusted dataset.
Choose open land away from obstacles, with road access and a grid or load nearby.
Check land rights, distance from homes and any aviation or radar limits.
A hilltop averages 6.5 m/s at 30 m height; a sheltered valley averages 4.2 m/s. The hilltop produces nearly four times the energy from the same turbine.
Tabulate monthly average wind speed for a real or practice site with the data source.
Table has twelve months, units and source.
Estimating energy
Apply
A simple estimate tells you if a project is worth a closer look.
Swept area = pi x radius squared.
Power in the wind = 0.5 x air density x area x speed cubed; real turbines capture only a fraction.
Annual energy = rated power x 8,760 hours x capacity factor.
Small turbines often reach 15 to 30 per cent capacity factor on good sites.
A 5 kW turbine at 22 per cent capacity factor produces 5 x 8,760 x 0.22 = about 9,636 kWh per year.
Calculate annual energy for your case and show every step with units.
Units and steps are correct, and the result is checked against the capacity factor range.
Turbine types and sizes
Analyse
Choose the right size and type for the site and the need.
Horizontal-axis turbines are most efficient; vertical-axis turbines are sometimes used where wind is turbulent, but usually produce less.
Small turbines suit remote sites; medium and large turbines suit farms and grids.
Grid-tied systems send extra power to the network; off-grid systems need batteries.
Compare cost per kW, noise, service needs and warranty.
A village chooses a grid-tied 10 kW turbine to reduce diesel use, rather than a 3 kW unit with batteries that would not meet its evening load.
Compare three turbines in a table with rated power, rotor diameter, cost per kW and notes.
Table is complete with sources and dates.
Cost and payback
Evaluate
Count the full cost and the full benefit.
Costs: turbine, tower, foundation, wiring, permits, installation, maintenance, insurance.
Benefit: electricity bills avoided or sold; value of backup.
Simple payback = total cost / yearly benefit.
Test with higher costs and lower wind to see how safe the case is.
Cost 6,50,000 INR; yearly benefit 85,000 INR; payback 7.6 years. If wind is 10 per cent lower, energy falls about 27 per cent and payback stretches past 10 years.
Build a payback sheet with a base case and a low-wind case.
Maths correct and the currency is shown.
Safety and maintenance
Apply
Heights, rotating parts and electricity are serious hazards.
Only trained and certified people work at height or on electrical systems.
Lock out and tag out before maintenance; never climb in strong wind.
Regular checks: bolts, blades, brakes, wiring and tower.
Keep the public away with fencing and signs.
A crew has a rule that nobody climbs if wind exceeds a set speed. The rule is posted at the base and checked on a log sheet.
Write a safety checklist and a monthly maintenance schedule.
Mentor engineer confirms the lists.
Environment and community
Evaluate
Projects work best when neighbours and nature are considered from the start.
Noise, shadow flicker, birds and bats, land use and views.
Consult neighbours early and follow permit rules.
Plan decommissioning and recycling at end of life.
Share benefits such as cheaper power or local jobs.
Seasonal shutdowns during peak bird migration, radar checks and a community benefit fund reduce objections.
List impacts and controls for a practice site.
Each impact has a control and an owner.
Write the feasibility note
Create
Bring it together into a clear decision note.
One-page summary with site, wind data, energy, cost and payback.
List assumptions and risks.
State what you do not know yet.
Have a mentor review.
The note recommends a one-year wind monitoring mast before buying a turbine, saving the risk of a poor site.
Write and present the note.
A peer can follow every number.
quiz: What does the generator do?
Turns rotation into electricity. (Covered in module 1: How a wind turbine works. To pass that module: All main parts are named and the cube rule is stated correctly.)
What happens to power when wind doubles?
About eight times more. (Covered in module 2: Wind resource and sites. To pass that module: Table has twelve months, units and source.)
Swept area formula?
Pi x radius squared. (Covered in module 3: Estimating energy. To pass that module: Units and steps are correct, and the result is checked against the capacity factor range.)
Typical small capacity factor?
15 to 30 percent. (Covered in module 4: Turbine types and sizes. To pass that module: Table is complete with sources and dates.)
Name a cost item.
Turbine, tower, foundation, wiring, permits, maintenance. (Covered in module 5: Cost and payback. To pass that module: Maths correct and the currency is shown.)
Payback formula?
Cost divided by yearly benefit. (Covered in module 6: Safety and maintenance. To pass that module: Mentor engineer confirms the lists.)
Who may work at height?
Trained, certified people. (Covered in module 7: Environment and community. To pass that module: Each impact has a control and an owner.)
Name two impacts.
Noise and birds (or shadow flicker). (Covered in module 8: Write the feasibility note. To pass that module: A peer can follow every number.)
Why a year of wind data?
To cover all seasons. (Covered in module 8: Write the feasibility note. To pass that module: A peer can follow every number.)
Why decommissioning plan?
To remove and recycle safely. (Covered in module 8: Write the feasibility note. To pass that module: A peer can follow every number.)
